blocks.content: A Kubernetes Namespace is a way to divide one physical cluster into multiple virtual sub-clusters, letting different teams, projects, or environments share the same underlying infrastructure without stepping on each other.

A Namespace is not a separate cluster, physically, it is all still the same nodes, the same control plane, but Namespaces give you a way to logically partition it, team-a and team-b can each have their own isolated slice of the same cluster.

blocks.alt: One physical cluster, logically divided into isolated slices

blocks.content:
kubectl create namespace team-a
kubectl get pods -n team-a

blocks.content: 2. Dividing Resources by Team, Project, or Environment
blocks.text: 2. Dividing Resources by Team, Project, or Environment

blocks.content: The most common real use is organizational, separate namespaces per team, per project, or per environment (dev, staging, production), all sharing one cluster's underlying compute while staying cleanly separated at the object level.

blocks.alt: A clean organizational boundary within one shared cluster

blocks.content: 3. Most Objects Are Namespaced, a Few Are Not
blocks.text: 3. Most Objects Are Namespaced, a Few Are Not

blocks.content: The overwhelming majority of object types, Pods, Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, live inside a specific namespace. A handful of object types, most notably the Persistent Volume covered in the Storage module, are cluster-scoped instead, existing above any single namespace.

blocks.alt: Most things live inside one namespace, a few important exceptions do not

blocks.content: If you never specify a namespace, whether with kubectl or in a manifest, objects land in a namespace literally called default, this is convenient for quick experimentation, but real production clusters almost always use dedicated, named namespaces instead.

blocks.alt: Where everything lands unless you say otherwise

blocks.content: 5. Not the Same as a Linux Namespace
blocks.text: 5. Not the Same as a Linux Namespace

blocks.content: This is genuinely worth clarifying explicitly, since the terminology overlap causes real confusion: a Kubernetes Namespace (this topic) is a cluster-organization concept, completely unrelated to a Linux kernel namespace (covered in the Docker Internals module), the mechanism that gives a container its isolated view of processes and networking. Same word, two entirely different ideas at two entirely different layers.

blocks.alt: The same word, describing two genuinely unrelated concepts

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: A Kubernetes Namespace divides one physical cluster into logical sub-clusters, most object types are namespaced, a few (like PV) are cluster-scoped instead.
This has nothing to do with Linux kernel namespaces from the Docker Internals module, the same word describes two completely unrelated concepts.
